Derivative-Free Optimization 4: Black Boxes¶

A black box is a function you can call but not look inside: a simulation, a solver run, a measurement. It may fail on some inputs, return several objectives, report constraints alongside, and cost seconds per call. This chapter covers the blackbox interface and the mesh adaptive solver behind it, MadsAdvanced. After it you can report failures honestly, use the cache, trade several objectives with weights, and choose how constraints are treated.

Every program is complete and its output is the output of that program.

The interface¶

Instead of objective, set blackbox. It returns a BlackboxEvaluation:

Field

Meaning

Default

objectives

one or more real values (a vector)

required

constraints

zero or more values, feasible when every entry is <= 0

none

evaluation_ok

false marks the call as a failure; its values are ignored

true

count_evaluation

false keeps the call out of the evaluation budget (use it for cheap pre-checks)

true

Setting blackbox makes Auto choose MadsAdvanced. You can also pass a blackbox to OrthoMads or LtMads, which share its machinery.

The options live in DfoOptions::mads:

Option

Meaning

Default

constraint_handling

Ignore, ExtremeBarrier, ProgressiveBarrier

Ignore

progressive_barrier_penalty

merit penalty per unit of violation

100

multiobjective_scalarization

WeightedSum or Chebyshev

WeightedSum

objective_weights, objective_reference

weights, and the reference point for Chebyshev

equal weights

enable_cache, cache_round_digits

remember evaluated points (rounded to this many digits)

on, 12

search_points

extra trial points per iteration before the poll

0

surrogate_mode

Off or CandidateOrdering (rank candidates with a cheap local model)

Off

Programs¶

  • Functions that fail and functions that are expensive

  • Several objectives and constraint policies

Checklist¶

  1. Report failures with evaluation_ok = false, not with a large number.

  2. Leave the cache on for deterministic functions.

  3. For several objectives, choose the weights deliberately and read the Pareto archive to see what else was found.

  4. Pick the constraint-handling policy to match the problem; with ProgressiveBarrier set the penalty above the objective’s slope.

  5. Verify constraints at the returned point.
